question: Define Riemann integration using Darboux sums. Prove that a bounded function $f:[a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ such that $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.
concept_tested: Darboux Definition of Riemann Integral and Integrability Criterion (Complete Essay)
approach: Define partitions, subintervals, $M_i, m_i$, Darboux sums $U(P, f), L(P, f)$, upper and lower integrals. State and prove the refinement lemma, then establish $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$ biconditional.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Definitions of Darboux Sums & Integrals
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta x_i, \quad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta x_i \quad \text{where } M_i = \sup_{I_i} f, \, m_i = \inf_{I_i} f
solution_steps.explanation: The upper integral is $\overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(P, f)$ and lower integral is $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(P, f)$. A bounded function is Riemann integrable if $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f = \int_a^b f$.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Refinement Property
solution_steps.math: P \subseteq P^* \implies L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f) \le U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Refining a partition cannot decrease lower sums nor increase upper sums. Furthermore, for any two partitions $P_1, P_2$, $L(P_1, f) \le U(P_2, f)$ by taking the common refinement $P^* = P_1 \cup P_2$.

solution_steps.title: Part 3: Forward Direction ($\implies$)
solution_steps.math: \underline{\int} f = \overline{\int} f = I. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists P_1 : L(P_1, f) > I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists P_2 : U(P_2, f) < I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction: Common Refinement
solution_steps.math: P = P_1 \cup P_2 \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) \le U(P_2, f) - L(P_1, f) < \left(I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) - \left(I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus there exists a partition $P$ with $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Part 4: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$)
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) \le \underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) \implies 0 \le \overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $0 \le \overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f < \epsilon$ for all $\epsilon > 0$, the non-negative difference must be 0, so $\overline{\int} f = \underline{\int} f$, proving $f$ is Riemann integrable.

final_answer: A bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a partition $P$ such that $U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon$.
exam_tip: In a 10-mark essay, clearly include the definitions, the common refinement lemma $L(P_1) \le U(P_2)$, and both directions of the biconditional.

question: State and prove the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First and Second Parts).
concept_tested: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First and Second Parts)
approach: State and prove FTC-1 ($F'(x) = f(x)$ for continuous $f$) using difference quotient, then prove FTC-2 ($\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$) using MVT and Darboux squeeze.

solution_steps.title: FTC Part 1 Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b], \quad F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt \quad (x \in [a, b])
solution_steps.explanation: Then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$. Furthermore, if $f$ is continuous at $c \in [a, b]$, then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ and $F'(c) = f(c)$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of FTC Part 1
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is continuous at $c$, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|t - c| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(c)| < \epsilon$. For $0 < |h| < \delta$:

solution_steps.title: Bounding Difference Quotient
solution_steps.explanation: Taking $h \to 0$ gives $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{h} = f(c)$, hence $F'(c) = f(c)$.

solution_steps.title: FTC Part 2 Statement & Proof
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b], \, F'(x) = f(x) \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: For any partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$, by the Mean Value Theorem on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, $\exists t_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ such that $F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(t_i)\Delta x_i = f(t_i)\Delta x_i$.

solution_steps.title: Summation and Darboux Squeeze
solution_steps.math: F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)\Delta x_i \implies L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, taking $\sup L(P, f) = \inf U(P, f) = \int_a^b f$ gives $\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$.

final_answer: FTC-1 establishes that differentiation reverses integration ($F'(c) = f(c)$); FTC-2 establishes that integration can be evaluated by an antiderivative ($\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$).
exam_tip: Clearly separate the hypotheses: FTC-1 assumes continuity of $f$ at point $c$; FTC-2 assumes $f$ has an antiderivative $F$ on $[a, b]$ and $f$ is integrable.

question: Prove that if a bounded function $f:[a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ has only a finite number of points of discontinuity, then $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
concept_tested: Riemann Integrability of Functions with Finitely Many Discontinuities / Substitution Theorem
approach: State and prove that if a bounded function $f:[a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous except at a finite number of points, then $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ bounded with discontinuities at } c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_k \implies f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: A bounded function on $[a, b]$ having only a finite number of points of discontinuity is Riemann integrable.

solution_steps.title: Single Discontinuity Case ($k = 1$)
solution_steps.explanation: Let $c$ be the single point of discontinuity. Enclose $c$ in an interval $[c - \delta, c + \delta]$ with $\delta < \frac{\epsilon}{8M}$.

solution_steps.title: Integrability on Outer Intervals
solution_steps.math: f \text{ continuous on } [a, c - \delta] \text{ and } [c + \delta, b] \implies \exists P_1, P_2 \text{ s.t. } U(P_1) - L(P_1) < \frac{\epsilon}{4}, \; U(P_2) - L(P_2) < \frac{\epsilon}{4}
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous functions on closed bounded intervals are Riemann integrable.

solution_steps.title: Combining Partitions
solution_steps.math: P = P_1 \cup P_2 \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \frac{\epsilon}{4} + 2M(2\delta) + \frac{\epsilon}{4} < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + 4M\left(\frac{\epsilon}{8M}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: The oscillation on the middle interval is at most $2M$, contributing $2M(2\delta) < \epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: General Case by Induction
solution_steps.math: \text{By additivity of integral over } [a, b] = [a, c_1] \cup [c_1, c_2] \cup \dots \cup [c_k, b], \quad f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is integrable on each subinterval with at most one endpoint discontinuity, it is integrable on $[a, b]$.

final_answer: Every bounded function with finitely many discontinuities on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
exam_tip: This theorem is a key consequence of Lebesgue's Criterion (a bounded function is Riemann integrable iff its set of discontinuities has measure zero).
